kurals.tamil:
அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை வேண்டும்
பெருமை முயற்சி தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arumai udaiththendru asaavaamai vendum
Perumai muyarchi tharum.
kurals.meaning: Never lose heart by telling yourself a task is too hard; it is effort itself that gives you the strength and stature to carry it through.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a big hill you have to climb to get home. If you stand at the bottom saying 'it’s too steep,' you never move. But every step you take makes your legs a little stronger, until the hill doesn’t look so big any more. Trying is what makes you able.
kurals.university: The chapter title ஆள்வினை (literally ‘man-work’, human exertion) is glossed by the Thirukkural-Thamizh edition as இடைவிடாத முயற்சி, ‘unceasing effort’, and this opening couplet names the first enemy of effort: அசாவு, the despondency that sets in when a task is judged அருமை (difficult). Parimelazhagar takes பெருமை not as fame but as the ‘greatness’ or capacity needed to accomplish the deed, so the claim is causal: capacity is produced by striving rather than being a precondition for it; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah (ytamizh.com) both read it this way, while Kalaignar renders பெருமை as ‘great strength’. Placed immediately after ஊக்கமுடைமை (ch. 60, energy) and மடியின்மை (ch. 61, absence of sloth), the chapter moves from inner zeal to its outward expression in sustained work, culminating in the famous claim of kural 620 that effort can turn back fate itself. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the latter printing the older sandhi-joined form (அருமை யுடைத்தென் றசாவாமை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “You should thus perform your prescribed Vedic duties, since action is superior to inaction. By ceasing activity, even your bodily maintenance will not be possible.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells the hesitant Arjuna that withdrawing from action is never the higher path; even keeping the body alive requires work.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita refuses to let the difficulty of a task become an excuse for not acting.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shared rejection of inaction, but the Gita speaks of prescribed duty, not of courage before a hard task.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges the Galatians not to grow tired of doing good, promising a harvest to those who do not give up.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Faint not’ is almost a translation of the Kural’s அசாவாமை, not sinking into weariness before the work is done.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on refusing to lose heart; Paul’s horizon is spiritual reward rather than worldly capacity.

islam.explanation: The short Meccan sura consoles the Prophet in difficulty by twice promising that ease comes together with hardship, then tells him to keep labouring (94:7).
islam.tie_back: Both texts tell the believer that a task’s hardness is not a reason to despair of it.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the anti-despair message; the Qur’an grounds it in divine promise rather than in effort’s own power.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you at liberty to neglect it”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon teaches that the vastness of a task does not release a person from the obligation to work at it.
judaism.tie_back: Tarfon and Valluvar both deny that ‘it is too great for me’ is a valid reason to hold back.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:16 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel; Tarfon speaks chiefly of Torah study, and releases one from finishing, which the Kural does not.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “You yourselves must strive; the Buddhas only point the way.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his followers that no teacher can do the work of liberation for them; the effort must be their own.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the verse locates the power to accomplish in one’s own striving, not in circumstances.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on self-reliant effort; the verse does not address a task’s difficulty directly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows: long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first; but when a man has reached the top, then is she easy to reach, though before that she was hard.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his idle brother Perses that excellence lies up a steep road that becomes easy only once one has climbed it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s ‘hard at first, easy at the top’ is the Kural’s point that effort creates the capacity the task seemed to demand.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 286-292 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near match; Hesiod speaks of virtue or prosperity broadly rather than of a single task.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca remarks to Lucilius that it is not because things are difficult that we do not dare; it is because we do not dare that they are difficult.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic argues that the difficulty we attribute to a task is largely produced by our own timidity toward it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly Valluvar’s warning against calling a thing ‘too hard’ and sinking into despondency.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close in thought; paraphrased because the English wording was not checked against a live text.

kurals.tamil:
வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல் வினைக்குறை
தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Vinaikkan vinaikedal ombal vinaikkurai
Theerndhaarin theerndhandru ulagu.
kurals.meaning: Once you are in the middle of a task, guard against letting your effort slacken; the world abandons those who abandon their work half-done.
kurals.elementary: If you start building a sandcastle and walk away halfway, the waves wash it away and nobody even knows what you were making. Friends want to team up with the kid who finishes things. Keep going until it’s done.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on வினை three times: in the course of வினை (the undertaking), guard against கெடல் (the failing) of வினை (the exertion), because the world has already தீர்ந்தது (let go of) those who have let go of வினைக்குறை, the unfinished remainder of the work. Parimelazhagar reads the first வினை as the undertaking and the second as the effort (முயற்சி), which Mu. Varadarasanar follows; Solomon Pappaiah paraphrases the rhetorical jingle of the second line (தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று) as ‘the world lets go of those who let go’. Kalaignar glosses it with the proverb of the man who ‘leapt half-way across the well’, a vivid way of saying that half an effort is no effort at all. The text agrees in both editions consulted, thirukkural-thamizh.org merely printing the sandhi forms வினைகெட லோம்பல் and தீர்ந்தாரிற் றீர்ந்தன் றுலகு.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka sorts people into three kinds: the lowest never begin a task for fear of obstacles, the middling begin but stop when obstacles strike, and the best, though struck again and again by obstacles, never abandon what they have begun.
hinduism.explanation: The famous Sanskrit verse (prārabhyate na khalu vighnabhayena nīcaiḥ) makes persistence through obstruction the mark of the noblest person.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s warning against letting effort fail midway is precisely Bhartrhari’s distinction between the middling and the best.
hinduism.source: Bhartrhari, Nitishataka (verse beginning prārabhyate na khalu)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close in thought; paraphrased because no verified English text was consulted, and verse numbering varies by edition.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that a half-built tower makes its builder a public laughing-stock, so one must be ready to see a commitment through.
christianity.tie_back: The mocking onlookers are the Kural’s ‘world’ that turns away from those who leave work unfinished.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close image of social disgrace for unfinished work; Jesus stresses counting the cost beforehand as well.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do good deeds properly, sincerely and moderately and know that your deeds will not make you enter Paradise, and that the most beloved deed to Allah is the most regular and constant even if it were little.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that steady, continuous action is dearer to God than bursts of effort that are then abandoned.
islam.tie_back: Both texts prize constancy of effort over enthusiastic beginnings that lapse.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the value of constancy; the hadith concerns devotional deeds, not worldly undertakings.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof; And the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth values the completion of a matter above its start, and patient endurance above proud self-assurance.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise measures a person by whether the work is carried to its end.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good thematic fit; the verse is a general maxim rather than a warning about abandoned work.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha recalls that he resolved: let skin, sinews and bones remain and flesh and blood dry up, but there would be no relaxing of his persistence until he had attained what can be reached by human firmness, human persistence and human striving.
buddhism.explanation: In the Anguttara Nikaya the Buddha names ‘not shrinking back in exertion’ as one of the two qualities that brought him to awakening.
buddhism.tie_back: The Pali purisa-viriya, ‘human (literally manly) effort’, is an exact counterpart of ஆள்வினை, and the refusal to relax midway is this kural’s whole point.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Striking verbal and thematic parallel; paraphrased since the translation was not re-checked here.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When some of Odysseus’ men eat the lotus and lose all wish to go home, he drags them weeping back to the ships and ties them under the benches so the voyage can go on.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Odyssey 9 the lotus-eaters’ gift is forgetfulness of the goal; Odysseus refuses to let the homeward labour stop halfway.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The lotus is the Kural’s வினைகெடல, the slackening of effort in mid-course, and Odysseus guards against it by force.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative image of refusing to abandon a task midway; not a moral teaching in form.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In every affair consider what precedes and follows, and then undertake it. Otherwise you will begin with spirit; but not having thought of the consequences, when some of them appear you will shamefully desist.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus warns that people who start eagerly without weighing the effort required give up in disgrace when difficulties appear, and compares them to children who play at one role after another but are nothing with their whole soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts call it shameful to drop a task halfway, though Epictetus places the remedy in weighing the work before starting rather than in keeping one's effort up once started.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Carter translation). Strong match on the disgrace of abandoning work begun; Epictetus stresses prior deliberation, the Kural stresses not slackening midway, and the Kural's point that the world abandons such people is absent.

kurals.tamil:
தாளாண்மை என்னும் தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்றே
வேளாண்மை என்னுஞ் செருக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thaalaanmai ennum thagaimaikkan thangitre
Velaanmai ennum serukku.
kurals.meaning: The proud distinction of being able to help others rests on one foundation only: the noble quality of hard work.
kurals.elementary: You can only share cookies with your friends if somebody baked them first. People who work hard are the ones who end up with something to give, and giving feels great. So working is what makes kindness possible.
kurals.university: தாளாண்மை, literally ‘the rule of the foot’, is Valluvar’s image for vigorous exertion, and வேளாண்மை here means beneficence or generosity to others (Parimelazhagar: உபகாரம்), not ‘agriculture’, its commonest modern sense. செருக்கு, usually ‘arrogance’, is used positively for the lofty eminence or noble pride of a benefactor, and the emphatic particle ஏ in தங்கிற்றே (‘it abides only there’) makes effort the exclusive seat of that eminence. The logic, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both preserve, links this chapter to the Arathuppal chapters on ஒப்புரவறிதல் and ஈகை: generosity is a virtue, but it presupposes the means that only labour produces. Kalaignar reads the couplet as describing people of ‘unceasing effort’ in whom the pride of helping others takes root. Both editions consulted agree on the text, apart from sandhi (தகைமைக்கட் டங்கிற்றே).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Riches and other objects of enjoyment do not follow the stingy, nor the impotent, nor the idler.”
hinduism.explanation: In Bhishma’s discourse on destiny and exertion, Brahma declares that prosperity eludes both the miser and the idle.
hinduism.tie_back: Linking the idler with the miser echoes the Kural’s claim that the power to give depends on the habit of effort.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section VI (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Connects idleness with lack of wealth; the benefactor’s pride is not addressed directly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells converts that honest labour has a purpose beyond self-support: it makes giving to the needy possible.
christianity.tie_back: Labour ‘that he may have to give’ is exactly the Kural’s claim that beneficence rests on effort.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match of the work-to-generosity link.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, spend from the good things which you have earned”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an asks believers to give in charity from their own honest earnings and from the produce of the earth.
islam.tie_back: Charity is spoken of as flowing from what one has earned, as the Kural roots beneficence in labour.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear link of earning and giving; the verse stresses the quality of what is given rather than effort itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: The ‘woman of valour’ of Proverbs 31 rises before dawn, works wool and flax with willing hands, buys a field and plants a vineyard from her earnings, and also opens her hand to the poor and needy.
judaism.explanation: The acrostic poem portrays a household sustained by tireless industry that overflows into generosity.
judaism.tie_back: Her open hand to the poor is made possible by her busy hands, as the Kural says generosity lives in effort.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; the poem praises a household manager rather than stating the principle.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who acquires his wealth in harmless ways like to a bee that honey gathers, riches mount up for him like ant hill’s rapid growth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the householder Sigala to gather wealth industriously and then divide it, keeping portions for use, business and need, and so win friends by liberality.
buddhism.tie_back: Industrious gathering followed by generous sharing mirrors the Kural’s chain from effort to beneficence.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shows the link between diligent earning and liberality; less emphasis on the pride of giving.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles’ labours, from killing the Nemean lion to clearing the Stymphalian birds, rid Greece of monsters and earned him cult as Alexikakos, ‘averter of evil’, a benefactor of humankind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tradition made Heracles’ glory inseparable from the gruelling toil through which he served others.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His honour as benefactor rests on his labours, as the Kural says the pride of helping others dwells in effort.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose parallel; Heracles’ labours were imposed as penance, not undertaken to fund generosity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says the liberal man will not neglect his own property, since he wishes by means of it to help others.
philosophy.explanation: In his account of liberality, Aristotle insists that true generosity requires caring for and maintaining one’s means.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers see generosity as dependent on the diligent management that produces the means to give.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in logic; paraphrased from Ross’s translation without a verbatim check.

kurals.tamil:
தாளாண்மை இல்லாதான் வேளாண்மை பேடிகை
வாளாண்மை போலக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thaalaanmai illaadhaan velaanmai pedikai
Vaalaanmai polak kedum.
kurals.meaning: A person who will not work but wants to be generous will fail, like a sword brandished by someone with no stomach for battle.
kurals.elementary: Holding a toy sword doesn’t make you a knight; you need the courage to use it. In the same way, saying ‘I’ll help everyone!’ doesn’t help anyone unless you are willing to do the work that makes helping possible.
kurals.university: The couplet sharpens kural 613 by negation: வேளாண்மை (beneficence) without தாளாண்மை (effort) is like the வாளாண்மை (sword-mastery) of a பேடி. Parimelazhagar and the older commentators take பேடி as a person of indeterminate sex, conventionally assumed in the ancient world to lack a warrior’s daring; Solomon Pappaiah softens this to ‘one who trembles at the sight of an army’, and the image is best read today as ‘a sword in the hand of one who dare not use it’, since the underlying gender assumption reflects its period rather than Valluvar’s point. The logic is that good intentions without the means produced by labour are as useless as a weapon one cannot wield; Mu. Varadarasanar says such generosity ‘will not come to fulfilment’. Both editions consulted agree on the wording; the sandhi form தாளாண்மை யில்லாதான் is purely orthographic.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Prince Uttara boasts to the palace women that he would rout the Kuru army if only he had a charioteer, but when he sees their host he leaps from the chariot and runs; it is his ‘eunuch’ dance-teacher Brihannala, really Arjuna in disguise, who takes up the bow.
hinduism.explanation: The Virata Parva episode contrasts loud promises of valour with the nerve and skill actually needed to act.
hinduism.tie_back: Uttara’s brave words without the grit behind them are the Kural’s empty sword-flourish; the tale’s irony, that the disguised ‘eunuch’ is the true hero, also undercuts the stereotype in the Kural’s image.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva (Go-harana), Sections XXXVI-XL (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Vivid narrative parallel for boast without capacity; concerns valour, not generosity.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?”
christianity.explanation: James mocks benevolent words that provide nothing real to the needy.
christianity.tie_back: Good wishes without the means to help are the Kural’s generosity that ‘perishes’ for want of effort.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on empty benevolence; James’s cause is lack of will to give, not lack of labour.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an asks believers why they say what they do not do, and declares it most hateful to God that people should say what they do not do.
islam.explanation: Surat as-Saff condemns a gap between professed intentions and actual deeds.
islam.tie_back: Both texts expose promises of good that are never backed by the work to fulfil them.
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel on words without deeds; the Qur’an’s context is readiness for struggle, not generosity.

judaism.quote_or_event: Shimon ben Gamaliel teaches that it is not study but doing that is the essential thing, and that whoever multiplies words brings on sin.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah places deeds above words or learning that never issue in action.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise judges good intentions worthless unless effort turns them into real help.
judaism._accuracy_note: General deeds-over-words parallel; does not address generosity or labour specifically.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada compares fine words that are not put into practice to a beautiful flower that has colour but no scent: they bear no fruit.
buddhism.explanation: Verses 51-52 contrast words that are merely spoken with words that are lived.
buddhism.tie_back: Kindly intent without effort is the Kural’s version of the scentless flower: attractive but fruitless.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Thematic parallel on fruitless good words; not about generosity or labour.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Paris strides out in gleaming armour to challenge the best of the Achaeans, but when Menelaus steps forward he shrinks back into the ranks, and Hector rebukes him as handsome to look at but lacking strength and courage.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Iliad 3 the splendid warrior-costume of Paris is exposed as show without substance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris is the Kural’s sword in an unwilling hand: the outward form of prowess with none of the effort behind it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close to the sword image itself; the Kural’s real subject, generosity without labour, is absent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that most people, instead of doing good acts, take refuge in theory and think they are being philosophers, like patients who listen carefully to their doctors but do none of the things prescribed.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that virtue is formed by doing, and that talking about goodness does not make anyone good.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats a will to do good without the effort behind it as ineffective.
philosophy._accuracy_note: General intention-versus-action parallel; not about generosity specifically.

kurals.tamil:
இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான் தன்கேளிர்
துன்பம் துடைத்தூன்றும் தூண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Inbam vizhaiyaan vinaivizhaivaan thankelir
Thunbam thudaiththoondrum thoon.
kurals.meaning: Someone who wants work rather than personal pleasure becomes a pillar for their family, wiping away their troubles and holding them up.
kurals.elementary: A house stands because of its pillars. They never get to go out and play; they just hold up the roof so everyone inside is safe. A person who chooses to work hard instead of just having fun becomes a pillar like that for their family.
kurals.university: The couplet contrasts two desires: இன்பம் விழையான் (one who does not crave his own pleasure) and வினை விழைவான் (one who craves the work). Such a man is a தூண் (pillar) that both துடைத்து (wipes away) and ஊன்றும் (props up) the sorrows of his கேளிர், his kin; Solomon Pappaiah widens கேளிர் to ‘relatives and friends’ and Kalaignar extends it to ‘the people of the country’, a modern civic reading. Parimelazhagar notes that the pillar image implies a household or lineage that would collapse without such a person. The couplet echoes the Arathuppal ideal of the householder (இல்வாழ்க்கை) as the support of all dependants, now reframed as a fruit of personal effort. Both editions agree on the wording, with sandhi-joined forms (வினைவிழைவான் றன்கேளிர்; துன்பந் துடைத்தூன்றுந் தூண்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna points to King Janaka and others who reached perfection through action, and urges Arjuna to work for lokasangraha, the holding-together and welfare of the world, rather than for himself.
hinduism.explanation: Bhagavad Gita 3.20 presents selfless work as the means by which the wise sustain society.
hinduism.tie_back: Work done for others’ sake, not one’s own pleasure, is the Kural’s pillar that holds up the kin.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the ideal of work for others’ welfare; the Gita’s horizon is the world, not the family.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.”
christianity.explanation: The pastoral letter makes providing for one’s household a basic duty of faith.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts make supporting one’s kin a central fruit of a working life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on duty to kin; the verse is a prohibition, the Kural an ideal portrait.

islam.quote_or_event: “The upper hand is better than the lower hand (i.e. he who gives in charity is better than him who takes it). One should start giving first to his dependents.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ranks the giver above the receiver and says generosity begins with those one supports.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s pillar is exactly this ‘upper hand’ that first sustains its own dependants.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on supporting dependants; the renunciation of pleasure is not mentioned.

judaism.quote_or_event: Joseph, having risen through years of labour in Egypt, tells his brothers he will sustain them in the famine, and then provides bread for his father, his brothers and all their households.
judaism.explanation: Genesis 45 and 47 show Joseph using his position to become the provider for his whole family.
judaism.tie_back: Joseph is the Kural’s pillar who wipes away his kin’s distress and holds them up.
judaism._accuracy_note: Apt narrative parallel; Joseph’s role owes as much to providence as to his own effort.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “But he who does not regard cold or heat any more than a blade of grass and who does his duties manfully, does not fall away from happiness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Sigala that the one who ignores comfort and discomfort alike and does his work well keeps his prosperity, and elsewhere lists supporting one’s parents as a son’s first duty.
buddhism.tie_back: Setting aside personal comfort to do one’s duties is the Kural’s man who desires work, not pleasure.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on renouncing comfort for duty; the ‘pillar for kin’ image is implicit rather than explicit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads the young Heracles meets two women: Vice offers him the easy road of pleasure, and Virtue the hard road of toil that brings real honour. He chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prodicus’ allegory, retold by Xenophon, made Heracles the model of choosing labour over ease.
greek_mythology.tie_back: ‘Not desiring pleasure but desiring work’ is exactly the choice of Heracles.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus, The Choice of Heracles, in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near-exact match on the first line; the support of kin is not part of the allegory.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius tells himself that when he is reluctant to rise at dawn he should remember he is rising to do the work of a human being, and asks whether he was made to lie warm under the blankets for his own pleasure.
philosophy.explanation: The emperor reminds himself that he exists for action and service, not for comfort.
philosophy.tie_back: Marcus chooses work over pleasure for the sake of others, as the Kural’s pillar does.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on preferring work to pleasure; the family-support image is absent.

kurals.tamil:
முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும் முயற்றின்மை
இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Muyarchi thiruvinai aakkum muyatrinmai
Inmai puguththi vidum.
kurals.meaning: Effort builds up prosperity; lack of effort ushers poverty in.
kurals.elementary: If you water a plant every day, it grows and gives you flowers. If you forget, it dries up. Effort is the water that makes good things grow, and not trying lets things wilt.
kurals.university: This is perhaps the most quoted couplet of the chapter, built on the paired opposites முயற்சி / முயற்றின்மை and ஆக்கும் / புகுத்திவிடும். Parimelazhagar reads திருவினை as திரு (wealth, prosperity) plus the empty increment இன் and the accusative ஐ, so ‘effort creates wealth’; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow this, whereas Sivayogi Sivakumar splits it as திரு + வினை, ‘auspicious deeds’, and Kalaignar as ‘excellent achievements’. இன்மை, ‘non-being’, is the standard Kural word for poverty (compare ch. 105, நல்குரவு), and புகுத்திவிடும் pictures idleness as actively ushering poverty into the house. The text is identical in both editions, thirukkural-thamizh.org printing the sandhi forms திருவினை யாக்கும் and யின்மை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A well-known verse of the Hitopadesha says that tasks are accomplished by effort, not by wishing, just as deer do not walk into the mouth of a sleeping lion.
hinduism.explanation: Even the lion, king of beasts, must hunt; desire alone never produces results (udyamena hi sidhyanti kāryāṇi na manorathaiḥ).
hinduism.tie_back: Both the fable-book and the Kural teach that effort alone brings gain, while idleness brings nothing.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match on effort versus inaction; paraphrased from the Sanskrit rather than checked against a translation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.”
christianity.explanation: Paul rebukes idlers in Thessalonica, telling them to work quietly and earn their own bread.
christianity.tie_back: Paul and Valluvar both tie livelihood directly to labour and want to idleness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match; Paul states a community rule rather than a law of cause and effect.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an lays down that a person’s portion is tied to his own striving (sa‘y).
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that what effort earns is what one has.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close in principle; the Qur’an’s primary reference is moral recompense, but it is widely applied to worldly effort.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In all labour there is profit; But the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb contrasts toil that yields gain with idle talk that leads to want.
judaism.tie_back: The same two-part structure as the Kural: labour brings profit, its absence brings poverty.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match in both thought and antithetical form.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Living in this way, he leaves many duties undone, new wealth he does not get, and wealth he has acquired dwindles away.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the excuses of the idle man, too cold, too hot, too early, too late, and states the economic result.
buddhism.tie_back: Idleness admitting poverty is the Kural’s second line in the Buddha’s words.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close on the poverty that idleness brings.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Through work men grow rich in flocks and substance, and working they are much better loved by the immortals.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod urges his brother Perses to work rather than seek wealth through lawsuits and idleness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod and Valluvar give the same economic law: work creates wealth.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 293-319 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close match on the first half of the couplet.

philosophy.quote_or_event: John Locke argues that it is labour that puts the difference of value on everything, reckoning that of the products useful to human life the far greater part is owed to labour rather than to nature.
philosophy.explanation: In his chapter on property, Locke makes labour the main source of wealth and value.
philosophy.tie_back: Locke gives a political-economic version of the Kural’s ‘effort produces wealth’.
philosophy.source: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, ch. 5, §40
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good thematic fit; Locke’s aim is to justify property, not to exhort effort.

kurals.tamil:
மடியுளாள் மாமுகடி என்ப மடியிலான்
தாளுளாள் தாமரையி னாள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Madiyulaal maamugadi enba madiyilaan
Thaalulaal thaamaraiyinaal.
kurals.meaning: The wise say the dark goddess of misfortune lives in laziness, while the lotus-goddess of fortune lives in the effort of the one who is not lazy.
kurals.elementary: Pretend Good Luck and Bad Luck are two visitors looking for a home. Bad Luck loves a messy room where someone is napping all day. Good Luck knocks on the door of the kid who’s busy building and practising. Where you work, good luck moves in.
kurals.university: Valluvar borrows two goddesses of popular belief: மாமுகடி, the ‘great dark Mugadi’ (மூதேவி, Sanskrit Jyeṣṭhā or Alakṣmī), goddess of misfortune, and தாமரையினாள், ‘she of the lotus’, Tirumagal or Lakshmi; the verb என்ப (‘they say’) signals that he is citing received wisdom. Parimelazhagar notes that sloth is the ‘dwelling’ of the one and effort (தாள்) the dwelling of the other, so fortune is located not in fate but in conduct; Kalaignar demythologises the pair entirely, treating the goddess names as figures for the industrious and the idle. There is a textual point: ytamizh.com prints தாளுளான் (masculine), but the parallelism with மடியுளாள் and the sandhi form றாளுளா டாமரையி னாள் in thirukkural-thamizh.org (தாளுளாள் + தாமரை) confirm the feminine தாளுளாள், ‘she dwells in the effort’, which is the reading adopted here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A famous Hitopadesha verse says that Lakshmi, goddess of fortune, approaches the lion-like man of effort, and only cowards say that fortune is handed out by fate; so set fate aside and exert yourself with your own strength.
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit maxim (udyoginaṃ puruṣasiṃham upaiti lakṣmīḥ) names the same goddess and the same condition for her favour.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural itself: the lotus-goddess comes to dwell with the diligent.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-identical image and teaching; paraphrased from the Sanskrit.

christianity.quote_or_event: In the parable of the talents, the servants who trade with their master’s money double it and are rewarded, while the one who buries his talent out of fear and sloth is called ‘wicked and slothful’ and loses even what he had.
christianity.explanation: Jesus’ parable shows increase coming to the active and loss to the idle.
christianity.tie_back: Blessing dwells with the diligent and deprivation with the lazy, as in Valluvar’s two goddesses.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on outcome; the parable concerns stewardship before God rather than personified fortune.

islam.quote_or_event: “Nobody has ever eaten a better meal than that which one has earned by working with one’s own hands. The Prophet of Allah, David used to eat from the earnings of his manual labor.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises self-earned sustenance as the best, citing even a prophet-king who lived by his own labour.
islam.tie_back: Blessing is found in one’s own labour, the ‘dwelling’ the Kural gives to the goddess of fortune.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the blessing-in-labour idea; no counterpart to the goddess of misfortune.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Yitzhak teaches that if someone tells you, ‘I laboured and did not find,’ do not believe him; ‘I did not labour yet found,’ do not believe him; but ‘I laboured and found,’ believe him.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud treats real attainment as something that only comes with toil.
judaism.tie_back: Success lodging only where there is labour is the Kural’s fortune that ‘dwells in effort’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in thought; the saying concerns Torah learning in context and is paraphrased here.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada links steadily increasing glory to energy and heedfulness.
buddhism.tie_back: Glory growing with the energetic parallels fortune taking up residence with the diligent.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on the positive half; the verse lists other virtues alongside energy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “work, high-born Perses, that Hunger may hate you, and venerable Demeter richly crowned may love you and fill your barn with food; for Hunger is altogether a meet comrade for the sluggard.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod pairs the grain-goddess Demeter, who favours the worker, with Hunger, the sluggard’s companion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Demeter and Hunger are an exact Greek counterpart to the lotus-goddess and the dark Mugadi.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 299-302 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Striking structural parallel: two divine figures allotted to the diligent and the lazy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Samuel Smiles opens Self-Help with the maxim ‘Heaven helps those who help themselves’, arguing that the spirit of self-help is the root of all genuine growth in the individual.
philosophy.explanation: The Victorian moralist made personal industry the true source of what people call good fortune.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Smiles says fortune favours the self-reliant worker.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good fit; Smiles quotes the maxim as proverbial rather than coining it.

kurals.tamil:
பொறியின்மை யார்க்கும் பழியன்று அறிவறிந்து
ஆள்வினை இன்மை பழி.
kurals.transliteration:
Poriyinmai yaarkkum pazhiyandru arivarindhu
Aalvinai inmai pazhi.
kurals.meaning: Bad luck is no disgrace to anyone; the real disgrace is knowing what should be done and still not making the effort.
kurals.elementary: Nobody laughs at you if it rains on sports day. That’s just bad luck. But if you knew you had a test and didn’t study at all, that’s on you. What matters is whether you tried.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on பழி (blame, disgrace) and on the contested word பொறி. Parimelazhagar takes பொறி as ஊழ், favourable destiny, so ‘to lack good fortune is no disgrace’; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar follow him, while Solomon Pappaiah (and, differently, Sivayogi Sivakumar) read பொறி in its other sense of bodily organ or faculty, making the point that physical disability is no disgrace but failure to exert oneself is. Both readings yield the same moral: blame attaches only to what lies in our power, namely அறிவறிந்து ஆள்வினை, effort guided by knowing what ought to be known. The chapter title word ஆள்வினை appears here explicitly, and the couplet prepares for 619-620’s direct confrontation with fate. The text is the same in both editions (sandhi: பழியன் றறிவறிந் / தாள்வினை யின்மை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Everything can be secured by Exertion: but nothing can be gained through Destiny alone, by a man that is wanting in personal Exertion.”
hinduism.explanation: Asked whether destiny or exertion is stronger, Bhishma relays Brahma’s answer that destiny is like seed and exertion like the tilled field, and neither yields without the other.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Mahabharata puts responsibility on the exertion that is within a person’s power.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section VI (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on the fate-versus-effort point; the blame and disgrace idea is implicit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him. I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.”
christianity.explanation: Asked whose sin caused a man’s blindness, Jesus denies that the affliction is anyone’s fault and turns at once to the duty of working while there is time.
christianity.tie_back: An unchosen affliction is no disgrace; neglecting the work one should do is what counts, as in the Kural, especially on Pappaiah’s ‘bodily faculty’ reading.
christianity._accuracy_note: Striking parallel on the first half; the second half concerns Jesus’ mission rather than ordinary effort.

islam.quote_or_event: “A strong believer is better and is more lovable to Allah than a weak believer, and there is good in everyone, (but) cherish that which gives you benefit (in the Hereafter) and seek help from Allah and do not lose heart, and if anything (in the form of trouble) comes to you, don’t say: If I had not done that, it would not have happened so and so, but say: Allah did that what He had ordained to do”
islam.explanation: The Prophet commands striving for what benefits and forbids losing heart, while accepting misfortune as decree rather than as grounds for self-reproach.
islam.tie_back: Misfortune is accepted without disgrace, but slackness in striving is not, which is the Kural’s own division.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close structure: accept decree, never neglect effort.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For a righteous man falleth seven times, and riseth up again, But the wicked stumble under adversity.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says the righteous are marked not by never falling but by rising again.
judaism.tie_back: Falling (misfortune) brings no shame; what matters is the effort to rise, as in the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Parallel on misfortune versus response; the verse contrasts the righteous and the wicked rather than effort and fate.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The idler who does not exert himself when he should, who though young and strong is full of sloth, with a mind full of vain thoughts — such an indolent man does not find the path to wisdom.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha condemns the one who has youth and strength and still will not exert himself at the right time.
buddhism.tie_back: Having capacity and knowing the time yet not striving is exactly the Kural’s ‘disgrace’.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on culpable non-effort; the verse does not discuss fate.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Work is no disgrace: it is idleness which is a disgrace.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells Perses that shame belongs not to labour or to poverty itself but to the idle.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod places disgrace precisely where Valluvar does: in the lack of effort.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 311 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near-verbatim echo of the second line; Hesiod does not mention fate here.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus begins his Handbook by dividing things into those within our power, our judgements, impulses and actions, and those not in our power, such as body, property and reputation.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, only what is in our power can be the object of praise or blame.
philosophy.tie_back: Unlucky externals carry no blame; neglecting what is in our power does, as the Kural says.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Same moral logic; Epictetus is about inner assent rather than outward effort.

kurals.tamil:
தெய்வத்தான் ஆகா தெனினும் முயற்சிதன்
மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Theyvaththaan aagaadhu eninum muyarchithan
Meyvaruththak kooli tharum.
kurals.meaning: Even if fate keeps the goal from being reached, effort will still pay the wages of the body’s toil.
kurals.elementary: Say you practise hard for a race and still don’t win because it rained and you slipped. You didn’t get the trophy, but your legs are stronger and you’re faster than before. Hard work always pays something, even when luck says no.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar glosses தெய்வம் as ஊழ் (fate, the fruit of past deeds), so the protasis concedes that destiny may make the full aim unattainable (ஆகாது); even then முயற்சி pays தன் மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி, the wage owed for its own bodily strain. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah keep the fate reading, but Kalaignar takes தெய்வம் literally as God, turning the couplet into a rationalist contrast between calling on God and working, a reading the Tamil can bear but the commentarial tradition does not support. The couplet is a careful concession to chapter 38 (ஊழ்), where kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate: Valluvar grants fate’s power over outcomes while denying it power to cancel the return on labour. Both editions agree, thirukkural-thamizh.org printing தெய்வத்தா னாகா தெனினு முயற்சிதன்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The body, the doer (soul), the various senses, the many kinds of efforts, and Divine Providence—these are the five factors of action.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists effort (ceṣṭā) and providence (daiva) as distinct contributors to any action, so neither alone determines the result.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita, like the Kural, gives effort its own share in outcomes even where fate also plays a part.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good analytic parallel; the Gita does not speak of a guaranteed ‘wage’ for toil.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.”
christianity.explanation: Paul assures the Corinthians that faithful labour is never wasted, whatever happens.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Not in vain’ is the Kural’s promise that effort always earns its wage.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on the assurance of reward; Paul grounds it in the resurrection rather than in effort itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that his effort is going to be seen - Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense”
islam.explanation: Following the verse that a person has only what he strives for, the Qur’an promises that every effort will be seen and fully repaid.
islam.tie_back: Effort is guaranteed its recompense, exactly the Kural’s ‘wage of toil’.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close; the Qur’an’s recompense is ultimately divine and eschatological.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ben He He said: According to the labor is the reward.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah’s terse Aramaic saying (lefum tza‘ara agra) ties reward to the pain of the labour.
judaism.tie_back: ‘According to the labour, the reward’ is the Kural’s ‘wage of the body’s toil’ almost word for word.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 5:23 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; Ben He He speaks mainly of Torah study and its reward.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Shipwrecked on his way to recover his kingdom, Prince Mahajanaka swims for seven days with no shore in sight. When the sea-goddess Manimekhala asks why he struggles in vain, he replies that one who strives does his duty and is free of blame even if he fails; moved, she carries him to safety.
buddhism.explanation: The Mahajanaka Jataka, one of the Ten Great Birth Stories, illustrates the perfection of energy (viriya).
buddhism.tie_back: Effort that seems doomed by fate still earns its reward, here literally, as the Kural promises.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Excellent narrative parallel; details paraphrased from the traditional story.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: A carter whose wagon is stuck in the mud prays to Heracles for help; the god appears and tells him to put his shoulder to the wheel and goad his oxen, for the gods help only those who help themselves.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Aesopic fable rebukes reliance on the gods in place of one’s own exertion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the fable says that effort, not appeal to heaven, gets results.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, Hercules and the Wagoner (Perry 291; trans. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close to Kalaignar’s God-versus-work reading; less so to Parimelazhagar’s fate reading.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant writes that even if, through the special disfavour of fortune or the meagre provision of a stepmotherly nature, a good will wholly lacked the power to achieve its purpose, it would still shine like a jewel by its own light, as something having its full worth in itself.
philosophy.explanation: For Kant the worth of a good will does not depend on whether fortune allows it to succeed.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers hold that adverse fortune cannot cancel the value of honest effort.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, Section I
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel; Kant speaks of moral worth, not of material return on labour.

kurals.tamil:
ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர் உலைவின்றித்
தாழாது உஞற்று பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Oozhaiyum uppakkam kaanbar ulaivindrith
Thaazhaadhu unjatru bavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who strive without faltering and without slackening will see even fate turn its back and retreat.
kurals.elementary: Think of a tiny stream running into a big rock. The rock seems stronger, but the water keeps flowing, day after day, until it carves a path around or even through. People who keep going without giving up can get past even the biggest ‘it’s just meant to be’.
kurals.university: The chapter ends with its boldest claim, the one most often quoted: tireless strivers will காண்பர் (see) the உப்பக்கம் (back, rear side) of ஊழ் (fate) itself, a battlefield image of an enemy turning its back in flight (Solomon Pappaiah: விதியையும் புறமுதுகு காட்டக் காண்பர்). The conditions are exacting: உலைவின்றி (without wavering), தாழாது (without delay or slackening) and உஞற்றுபவர் (those who exert themselves, an old verb for effort). Because chapter 38 insists on ஊழின் பெருவலி (fate’s great strength, kural 380), commentators have laboured to reconcile the two; Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar soften the claim so that strivers defeat the fate that obstructs a particular undertaking ‘in time’, while Kalaignar reads it as an outright rejection of fatalism. The couplet stands in the same Indian debate as the Mahabharata’s daiva-versus-puruṣakāra discussions and the Yoga Vasishtha’s praise of paurusha; the text agrees in both editions (sandhi: ஊழையு முப்பக்கங் காண்ப ருலைவின்றித் / தாழா துஞற்று பவர்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Yoga Vasishtha, Vasishtha tells Prince Rama that what people call fate (daiva) is nothing but the fruit of their own past effort, and that vigorous present effort (paurusha) can overcome it, as the stronger of two fighting rams prevails.
hinduism.explanation: The Mumukshu section devotes several chapters to arguing that self-effort, not destiny, is the decisive force in human life.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the fullest Sanskrit statement of the Kural’s claim that relentless effort can put fate to flight.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close in doctrine; paraphrased, and chapter numbering varies between recensions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes his life as an unrelenting forward effort that refuses to be defined by the past.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s tireless ‘pressing on’ is the Kural’s உலைவின்றித் தாழாது, striving without faltering or slackening.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the unrelenting effort; Paul does not claim to overcome fate.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an makes a people’s own inner change the condition on which their fortunes are transformed.
islam.tie_back: Human effort as the hinge of changed destiny is the Kural’s point, though framed within divine decree.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong parallel; the same verse also stresses that God’s decree cannot be repelled.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel; for thou hast striven with God and with men, and hast prevailed.”
judaism.explanation: After wrestling all night with a mysterious being and refusing to let go, Jacob is renamed for his striving.
judaism.tie_back: Jacob’s victory through unrelenting struggle with a superhuman power is the Kural’s striver who makes fate turn its back.
judaism._accuracy_note: Powerful narrative parallel; the Genesis story is about blessing, not fate as such.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “By effort and heedfulness, discipline and self-mastery, let the wise one make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that effort builds a refuge that the flood of circumstance cannot sweep away.
buddhism.tie_back: An island built by effort that no flood can overwhelm matches the Kural’s effort that stands firm against fate.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good parallel; the ‘flood’ is chiefly the defilements rather than fate.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Although Poseidon pursues him with storms and shipwreck for ten years, Odysseus keeps striving through every disaster and finally reaches Ithaca, winning his homecoming in the teeth of a god’s hostility.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Odyssey shows sustained human endurance prevailing against a hostile divine power.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus is the Greek image of the Kural’s striver who outlasts adverse fate.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good narrative parallel; Athena’s help and Zeus’s will also bring him home.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli judges that fortune may be arbiter of half our actions but leaves the other half to us, and compares her to a flooding river against which prudent men build dykes and embankments in calm times.
philosophy.explanation: In The Prince, ch. 25, he rejects fatalism and argues that energetic foresight (virtù) can check fortune.
philosophy.tie_back: Machiavelli’s dyke-building against fortune is a Renaissance version of the Kural’s effort that routs fate.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on effort versus fortune; Machiavelli concedes fortune half, the Kural claims more.
